key_insight: Channel geometry alone can strongly tune capillary-driven flow and analyte confinement in paper-based microdevices, with circular channels flowing fastest and diverging-converging channels slowest.
engineering_relevance: Geometry-guided channel design offers a practical way to control passive transport and preconcentration in low-cost paper diagnostics without external pumps.
method: Compared five paper-channel geometries: converging-diverging, diverging-converging, wide-to-narrow, circular, and rectangular.
Used geometry-adapted Lucas–Washburn analysis to model capillary flow.
Validated flow fields with CFD and UV fluorescence measurements of pyrene and benz[α]anthracene, plus cyclodextrin-functionalized chitosan for analyte retention.
evidence_signal: Experiments showed transport times ranging from 23.1 s (circular) to 65.0 s (diverging-converging), with CFD reproducing the observed velocity distributions and agreeing semi-quantitatively with model predictions.
watch_item: The findings are geometry- and coating-specific, so performance may shift with different paper porosity, surface chemistry, or analyte properties.
paper_title: Geometry-Driven Passive Fluid Transport in Paper-Based Microdevices
